The diagram shows the organization’s structure, not the customer.
It oversees the whole set and decides what gets funded.

questions.p: Very large or long-running products may have life cycle phases complex enough to need a set of programs and projects working together. Which form of product management is this?
o: Program management within a product life cycle
Coordinated programs and projects within a phase of a big product’s life is this form.
Portfolio management isn’t one of the three forms on these slides.
Project management within a product life cycle
This form charters individual projects, with no coordinated program.
Here the product’s life is inside a program, which is the other way round.

questions.p: A company modernizes a large product years after launch through several related, coordinated projects. Which form is this?
o: General management runs ongoing operations, not this temporary set of projects.
The product existed long before this work, and it isn’t contained in a program.
Program management within a product life cycle
Several related, coordinated projects make it a program, inside the product’s life.
Project management within a product life cycle
This form would be one individual project at a time, not a coordinated set.

questions.p: This approach “incorporates related projects, subsidiary programs, and program activities.” Which form does that describe?
o: This is what charters projects, not a form of product management.
Program management within a product life cycle
This is the slide’s description of this form.
That one applies the full life cycle within a program’s boundaries.
Project management within a product life cycle
That one oversees development as an ongoing activity, chartering individual projects.

questions.p: After five years, a company charters a single project to modernize its app’s user interface. Which form of product management is this?
o: This product isn’t contained within one program.
Project management within a product life cycle
One individual project, chartered as needed, is this form. The slide uses this exact example.
Program management within a product life cycle
That would need a set of coordinated programs and projects.
The portfolio charters the project, but it isn’t one of the three forms.

questions.p: In this form, what oversees the development and maturing of product capabilities?
o: Auditors check compliance. They don’t manage product development.
A temporary team that closes when the first version ships
That would be one project, and this form continues throughout the product’s life.
It is managed as an ongoing business activity
The slide’s wording is “as an ongoing business activity”.
Customers give feedback, but the organization runs this activity.

questions.p: Who charters the individual projects in this form?
o: A team doesn’t authorize its own project.
The slide says portfolio governance charters them as needed.
Customers may request changes, but they don’t charter internal projects.
PMI sets standards and doesn’t authorize a company’s projects.

questions.p: A program develops a proof of concept to explore possible directions, then ends it. Which form of product management is this?
o: Program management within a product life cycle
There, the product is larger than the program.
The small product’s full life cycle fits inside the program, and the slide uses this example.
A POC is a temporary, unique effort rather than ongoing work.
Project management within a product life cycle
There, an ongoing product charters individual projects.

questions.p: “Applies the full product life cycle within the purview and boundaries of a given program” describes:
o: This isn’t one of the three forms.
Program management within a product life cycle
Project management within a product life cycle
This form doesn’t have the product’s life contained in a program.

questions.p: In “product management within a program”, what contains what?
o: Programs contain projects, not the reverse.
The product’s life cycle contains the program
This describes program management within a product life cycle.
The program contains the product’s whole life cycle
The program is the outer box.

questions.p: The principles of project management are prescriptive rules that must be followed exactly.
o: In some professions principles are rules, but the slide says project management’s aren’t. They guide behavior, and there are many ways to stay aligned with them.
They are not prescriptive; they guide behavior and can be applied in many ways.

questions.p: Project management principles always reflect morals.
o: Watch out for “always”. A principle like tailoring is practical advice, with nothing moral about it.
The slide says they “can, but do not necessarily” reflect morals.

questions.p: What do principles for a profession serve as?
o: That describes a method or a process, not a principle.
Foundational guidelines for strategy, decision making, and problem solving
This is the slide’s first point. Standards and methods often build on them.
Some professions treat them as laws, but it isn’t universal, and project management doesn’t.
Principles guide behavior. They don’t set targets.

questions.p: Two PMs both apply “engage stakeholders” differently: weekly demos and monthly reviews. What does this show?
o: The principle has been violated by both
Both are engaging stakeholders, so both are aligned.
Principles are broad, so there are many ways to stay aligned with them
The slide says they’re broadly based, giving room for different approaches.
One PM is wrong, since principles allow only one way
Principles apply only in large organizations

questions.p: Which of the following is NOT one of the four values of the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct?
o: This is one of the four values.
This is one of the four values.
Integrity belongs to stewardship (slide 59). The four values are responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty.
This is one of the four values.

questions.p: A code of ethics is related to:
o: Ethics goes beyond law to what is right and wrong.
A code of ethics is about conduct, not schedules.
The slide says a code of ethics is related to morals, setting expectations for moral conduct.
These measure deliverables, not moral conduct.

questions.p: A PM discloses that a bidding vendor belongs to her cousin and steps out of the decision. Which value is she mainly applying?
o: She acts responsibly, but the main value here is keeping the decision impartial.
Avoiding a conflict of interest and staying impartial is fairness.
Respect concerns how people are treated. The issue here is impartiality.
She is honest in disclosing, but stepping out of the decision is what protects fairness.

questions.p: A PM admits to the client that a mistake in her own estimate caused the delay. Which value is this mainly?
o: Respect concerns how she treats others.
Owning your decisions and their consequences is responsibility.
Nobody is being treated impartially here.
Stewardship is a principle, not one of the four ethics values.

questions.p: A PM listens carefully to a junior developer’s concerns and doesn’t talk over them. Which value is this?
o: Nothing here is about telling the truth.
Nothing here is about owning results.
This could be fair, but the behavior described is how she treats the person.
Treating people with care and taking them seriously is respect.

questions.p: A PM reports the true status to the sponsor although the news is bad. Which value is this?
o: Respect matters, but what’s being tested is truthfulness.
Integrity isn’t one of the four values on this slide.
Telling the truth even when it is uncomfortable is honesty.
Nobody’s interests are being weighed against another’s.

questions.p: A code of ethics can be adopted by an individual or a profession to establish expectations for moral conduct.
o: The slide says both can adopt it.
The statement is correct: the slide says it can be adopted by an individual or by a profession.

questions.p: Because the principles are internally consistent, no practical dilemmas can arise when applying them.
o: Consistent doesn’t mean easy. The slide’s example is disclosing information versus keeping it confidential.
The principles don’t contradict each other, but the slide says practical dilemmas may still arise.

questions.p: “The principles are internally consistent” means:
o: No principle contradicts any other principle
This is the slide’s explanation of the phrase.
They apply in the same way on every project
They never overlap with general management
The slide says they can overlap.
They must be applied in numerical order

questions.p: Which of these influences the degree and way principles are applied?
o: The context of the organization, project, deliverables, team, and stakeholders
The slide lists these factors, since principles provide guidance rather than rules.
Only the size of the budget
Budget may matter, but the slide’s list is much wider.
The numerical order of the principles
PMI doesn’t rule on individual projects.

questions.p: Sharing a client’s data would help the team analyze the system, but the data is confidential. What does the slide call this?
o: The slide gives almost this exact example of disclosure versus confidentiality.
This concerns a confidentiality decision, not product management.
The slide says the principles don’t contradict each other.

questions.p: Project management principles can have areas of overlap with general management principles.
o: The slide says so, and the next slide illustrates it.
The statement is correct: it’s the last point on the slide.

questions.p: What does the Venn diagram show?
o: Project management principles and general management principles partly overlap
Two circles sharing a middle means some principles apply to both.
Project management is a part of operations
The diagram compares principles, not departments.
The shared middle area contradicts this.
Identical would mean complete overlap, but each also has its own area.

questions.p: A manager runs a permanent finance department with long-term staff and direct authority over them. This is closer to:
o: Ongoing work, permanent staff and line authority are its marks.
A PM has temporary work and usually a borrowed team.
This oversees a portfolio, not one department’s daily work.
A program coordinates related projects, which isn’t what’s described.

questions.p: “Recognize, evaluate, and respond to system interactions” is the full statement of which principle?
o: Slide 21’s “Systems Thinking” is this principle’s short name.
Tailoring’s statement is “Tailor based on context”.

questions.p: Which principle’s full statement is “Be a diligent, respectful, and caring steward”?
o: Stakeholders’ statement is “Effectively engage with stakeholders”.
Team’s statement is “Create a collaborative project team environment”.

questions.p: “Enable change to achieve the envisioned future state” matches which short name?
o: The statement uses the word directly.
This one’s statement is “Embrace adaptability and resiliency”.

questions.p: Which is an official PMI principle statement?
o: Follow the same process on every project
The real principle says to tailor based on context.
The real statement is “Optimize risk responses”. Not all risks can or should be eliminated.
Inspect quality at the end of the project
The actual statement says to build it in, not check at the end.
Build quality into processes and deliverables
This is one of the 12 statements on the slide.

questions.p: Which is NOT one of the four things stewardship includes?
o: This is one of the four.
This is one of the four.
The four are integrity, care, trustworthiness and compliance. Finance matters, but profitability isn’t on that list.
This is one of the four.

questions.p: A PM refuses to use personal data in a way that breaks privacy law, even though it would save money. Which part of stewardship is this mainly?
o: She may be trustworthy, but what’s described is following the law.
Compliance with internal and external guidelines
Following outside laws is compliance, even at a cost.
She isn’t adapting a method. She’s following the law.
Her choice reduces savings, so it isn’t about maximizing value.

questions.p: A holistic view of stewardship considers:
o: It includes technical matters, but goes much further.
Financial, social, technical, and sustainable environmental awareness
That would be a narrow view, not a holistic one.
Stewardship looks more widely, including outside the organization.

questions.p: Stewardship covers responsibilities only within the organization.
o: The card says “within and external to”, which is why environmental and social impacts count.
It covers responsibilities within and external to the organization.

questions.p: A team agrees on its own way of running stand-ups and reviewing code. What is this called on the card?
o: Governance concerns authority and rules at a higher level.
Teams often create their own culture within organizational and professional ones.
A local culture works within the guidelines.
This concerns the team’s habits, not the product.

questions.p: Which is NOT one of the things a collaborative team environment facilitates?
o: Removing the need for organizational guidelines
The card says it supports alignment with guidelines, which is the opposite.
Optimal contributions to deliver desired outcomes
Individual and team learning and development

questions.p: Project teams that work collaboratively can accomplish a shared objective more effectively and efficiently than individuals working on their own.
o: This is the card’s statement of the principle.
The statement is correct: it’s the card’s main statement.

questions.p: A PM discovers a department head will be affected, and meets with them before any complaint arises. Which words from the card does this show?
o: Going to them before problems arise is proactive engagement.
Tailoring adapts methods. This is about reaching out to a person.
Nothing about this involves uncertainty or interactions between factors.
No rule is being followed here.

questions.p: All stakeholders should be engaged in the same way and to the same degree.
o: Engagement should match each stakeholder’s needs and influence. Treating everyone equally wastes time and neglects those who matter most.
The card says to engage them “to the degree needed”.

questions.p: According to the card, stakeholder engagement:
o: Stakeholders define value, so engaging them helps deliver it.
Stakeholders include people inside and outside the organization.
Should wait until deliverables are complete
Proactive means early, not at the end.

questions.p: Stakeholders influence projects, performance, and outcomes.
o: This is the first point on the card.
The statement is correct: it’s the card’s first point, and the reason engagement matters.

questions.p: What is the ultimate indicator of project success, according to the card?
o: Being under budget doesn’t guarantee useful results.
Deliverables are means to outcomes and value.
The card’s wording: value is the ultimate indicator of project success.
A project can be on time and yet deliver little worth having.

questions.p: Value can be realized only at the end of a project.
o: The card lists three timings. Teams that release in increments deliver value along the way, for example.
It can be realized throughout the project, at its end, or after it’s complete.

questions.p: A project’s benefit is that “customers trust us more”, with no number attached. According to the card, this is:
o: This is about how value is defined.
Trust is a result, not an artifact.
Not real value, since it can’t be measured in money
Acceptable, since value can be defined in quantitative and/or qualitative terms
Value doesn’t have to be numeric.

questions.p: Midway through, a team drops a feature because the market has changed, and builds one that users now need more. Which principle is this?
o: Continually evaluating and adjusting alignment with benefits and value is this principle.
This isn’t about the quality of what’s produced.
The decision here is mainly about what’s worth building.
That’s about helping people adopt the new state. Here the team is adjusting what it builds.

questions.p: What does a focus on outcomes allow project teams to do, according to the card?
o: Support the intended benefits that lead to value creation
This is the card’s wording, and it matches the value chain on slide 34.
The card says nothing like this.

questions.p: A team discovers that changing the database will affect the payment system and the registration system. Which principle is most directly demonstrated?
o: Recognize, Evaluate, and Respond to System Interactions
A project is a system of interdependent parts; seeing how one change ripples into others is systems thinking.
Build Quality into Processes and Deliverables
Quality is about meeting requirements and acceptance criteria. The point here is one change affecting other parts.
Nobody’s leadership is being described in this scenario.
The team isn’t judging what is most worthwhile. It’s tracing effects across parts of the system.

questions.p: Systems need attention only once, during project planning.
o: Since systems keep changing, attention must be continuous, not limited to planning.
The card says systems are constantly changing, so they require consistent attention.

questions.p: How does the card describe a project?
o: This could describe a portfolio. A project’s parts are interrelated.
The parts depend on each other.
A system of interdependent and interacting domains of activity
A project has many parts, not one deliverable.

questions.p: A team notices another team’s new service could also solve its own problem, and reuses it. What does the card call this?
o: Reusing existing work doesn’t add requirements.
This is making use of an opportunity, not avoiding a threat.
Being responsive to system interactions to leverage positive outcomes
Responding to interactions isn’t only about avoiding damage. It can also bring gains.

questions.p: Systems thinking looks at how project parts interact with each other and with:
o: The card says “with each other and with external systems”.
It goes well beyond the plan.
It looks at the whole system.
It covers far more than money.

questions.p: Only the project manager can demonstrate leadership behaviors.
o: Leadership is different from authority, so a junior developer can lead without any formal power.
The card says any project team member can demonstrate them.

questions.p: Leadership is the same thing as authority.
o: Authority is a formal right. Leadership is getting people to follow, which can happen with or without it.
The card says leadership is different from authority.

questions.p: A leader gives detailed guidance to a new graduate and free rein to a senior engineer. Which point on the card does this show?
o: This is inconsistent, and leaders must treat everyone identically
Effective leaders adapt their style to the situation
Style changes with who and what you’re dealing with.
Tailoring concerns project methods, not individual style.
Leadership is the same as authority
This isn’t about authority at all.

questions.p: A PM rewards one person with public recognition and another with chances to learn. What does this show?
o: Adapting to what motivates people isn’t unfair.
Recognizing differences in motivation among team members
The card says effective leaders recognize these differences.
Nothing here concerns too much change.

questions.p: A PM asks the team to report honestly, and she herself openly reports her own errors. Which point does this show?
o: Leaders demonstrate desired behavior in honesty, integrity and ethical conduct
Setting the example is what the card asks for.
True in general, but the scenario illustrates setting an example.
True, but the scenario is about setting an example.

questions.p: Effective leadership promotes project success and contributes to positive project outcomes.
o: This is the card’s first point.
The statement is correct: it’s the first point on the card.

questions.p: Tailoring is a one-time activity performed when the project is initiated.
o: The card calls tailoring iterative and continuous. Teams adjust as they learn, rather than deciding once at the start.
Tailoring is iterative and continuous throughout the project.

questions.p: What does “just enough” process mean on this card?
o: The minimum paperwork the team feels like doing
It’s measured against achieving the outcome, not against how the team feels.
Enough process to achieve the outcome while maximizing value, managing cost, and enhancing speed
It’s a balance: no more process than is useful, and no less.
Using every process in the PMBOK
That is the opposite of tailoring.

questions.p: A team working on a regulated medical system keeps formal sign-offs, while a startup team skips them. Both succeed. What does this show?
o: Project success is based on adapting to the project’s unique context
Each chose the approach that fit its context.
One of the teams must be breaking the standard
The standard expects methods to differ.
They’re appropriate in a regulated context.
They need just enough for their context, not necessarily none.

questions.p: What should the development approach be designed around, according to the card?
o: Whichever method the PM has used most recently
Familiarity isn’t the basis the card names.
The context of the project, its objectives, stakeholders, governance, and environment
These are the things the card lists.
Cost is one consideration, but the card asks for much more.

questions.p: Each project is unique.
o: This is the first point on the card, and the reason tailoring is needed.
The statement is correct: it’s the card’s first point.

questions.p: Project quality focuses on meeting which of the following for deliverables?
o: The card says quality focuses on meeting acceptance criteria for deliverables.
Quality is judged against agreed criteria, not preferences.
Cost matters, but it isn’t what quality measures.

questions.p: Quality applies only to deliverables, not to the processes used to create them.
o: The principle’s name says “processes and deliverables”. Both count.
The card includes ensuring project processes are appropriate and as effective as possible.

questions.p: A team finds a requirement misunderstanding in a design review, rather than after launch. Which idea does this show?
o: Building quality in, rather than checking only at the end
Catching it early is what building quality into the process achieves.
Nothing here concerns too much change.
Risk appetite is how much risk an organization accepts.
Tailoring adapts methods, whereas this is about finding the defect early.

questions.p: What does project quality entail, according to the card?
o: The principle asks you to build quality in throughout.
Satisfying stakeholders’ expectations and fulfilling project and product requirements
Nothing on the card says this.
Exceeding every requirement regardless of cost
Quality is about meeting needs, not exceeding everything.

questions.p: Which of the following is NOT a source of complexity listed on the card?
o: The card lists human behavior, system interactions, uncertainty and ambiguity.

questions.p: Complexity can only emerge during the planning stage of a project.
o: The card says “at any point”, which is why teams must stay alert throughout.
It can emerge at any point during the project.

questions.p: Requirements are written so vaguely that different teams understand them differently. Which source of complexity is this?
o: No parts are interacting in this example.
People are involved, but the cause is the unclear wording.
The meaning itself is unclear, which is ambiguity.
Uncertainty is not knowing what will happen. Here it’s about what things mean.

questions.p: A team splits a large, confusing project into smaller prototypes to learn as it goes. What is this an example of?
o: You can reduce it, but not get rid of it.
Using methods to reduce the amount or impact of complexity
The card says teams use a variety of methods to do this.
The goal hasn’t been reduced, only broken into parts.
Nothing here concerns how much risk the organization accepts.

questions.p: Which of these can introduce complexity, according to the card?
o: It’s one of six items on the list.
Budget isn’t even on the list.
Laws aren’t specifically on this list, and it’s much wider.
Events affecting value, scope, communications, stakeholders, risk, or technological innovation

questions.p: In project management, risks are always negative.
o: The card includes both. A risk of a supplier delivering early is an opportunity you could use.
Risks can be positive (opportunities) or negative (threats).

questions.p: A team spends $50,000 protecting against a risk that could cost at most $2,000. Which response test does this fail?
o: The response costs far more than the damage it protects against.
Nothing here concerns who owns it.
It may be possible to do it. The problem is that it isn’t worth it.

questions.p: A risk response is agreed, but nobody is named to carry it out. Which test does this fail?
o: It could be realistic, but no one is assigned.
Every response needs a named owner.

questions.p: A team’s plan to “hire ten experts next week” for a small project with no budget fails which test?
o: The issue here is feasibility rather than agreement.
The response can’t be achieved given the project’s situation.
The main problem is that it can’t be done.

questions.p: A team has a response plan that the client strongly objects to. Which test does this fail?
o: Its fit to the risk isn’t what’s being objected to here.
Relevant stakeholders must accept the response.
Nothing here says it has no owner.

questions.p: Hiring a full security team to guard against a minor typo in a help page fails which test?
o: Appropriate for the significance of the risk
A response should match how much the risk matters.
It might be doable, but it’s out of proportion.

questions.p: A hospital accepts far less risk than a startup does. What explains this, according to the card?
o: They have many, and they treat them cautiously.
An organization’s risk attitude, appetite, and threshold influence how risk is addressed
Different organizations accept different levels of risk.
Risks are only addressed in startups

questions.p: When are risks addressed, according to the card?
o: That would be reacting rather than managing risk.
New risks can appear at any time, so it can’t be a one-time task.
Only at the end, in lessons learned
By then it’s too late to respond.

questions.p: A critical server failure takes the test environment down, and the team restores it from backups and resumes work within a day. Which quality does this show?
o: Stewardship concerns responsible and ethical behavior.
Adaptability responds to changed conditions. Here the team recovers from a failure and carries on as before.
Tailoring adapts methods to the context, which isn’t what’s happening here.
Absorbing an impact and recovering quickly from a setback is resiliency.

questions.p: A new regulation means the team must change its data-storage design midway through. It redesigns and continues. Which quality does this show?
o: Compliance may be stewardship, but the action described is changing the plan in response.
Nothing failed here, and there was no setback to recover from. Conditions changed.
Responding to changing conditions is adaptability.
The design change isn’t about quality.

questions.p: Which helps a project adapt, according to the card?
o: Longer planning with no changes allowed
This is the opposite of adaptability.
A fixed list of outputs that can’t change
A focus on outcomes rather than outputs
If the goal matters more than the original feature list, you can change the route to it.
This would make it harder to know what needs to change.

questions.p: Resiliency is the ability to absorb impacts and to recover quickly from a setback or failure.
o: The statement is correct: it’s the definition on the card. Compare it with adaptability, which is about responding to changing conditions.

questions.p: A ministry rolls out a new ERP, a new HR system and a new workflow in the same month. Staff start ignoring announcements and avoiding the new tools. What is happening?
o: Change fatigue, from attempting too much change in a short time
The card warns that too much change in a short time can lead to change fatigue and/or resistance.
The scope isn’t growing. The problem is people’s reaction to the pace of change.
The problem is with people, not servers.
Nobody is choosing to accept a risk here.

questions.p: What should the PM do in that situation, according to the card?
o: Pace the changes and use stakeholder engagement and motivational approaches
The card says engagement and motivation assist adoption.
Add more changes while people are adjusting
This is the cause of the problem.
Ignore the staff’s reaction, since the systems were delivered
A delivered system nobody uses creates no value.

questions.p: All stakeholders will embrace a change if it benefits the organization.
o: People may lose familiarity, status or comfort, so resistance can happen even when a change is good for the organization.
The card says enabling change can be challenging, as not all stakeholders embrace it.

questions.p: Change can originate from:
o: Change can also come from outside the organization.
A new law or a new CEO can also bring change.
Customers are one possible source among many.

questions.p: What does a structured approach to change help with?
o: The aim is to move to a new state.
Helping individuals, groups, and the organization move from the current state to the desired future state

questions.p: Months after go-live, staff are slowly going back to the old spreadsheets. Which word on the card addresses this?
o: The problem is people sliding back rather than the process fit.
The system was accepted. People aren’t staying with it.
This doesn’t explain why they’re returning to old habits.
The card says to prepare people for adoption and sustainment , so the change has to last.

questions.p: Which of the following best explains the nature of project performance domains?
o: They represent distinct areas of focus that guide effective project management.
Performance domains are areas of focus that run concurrently; they are not sequential processes or deliverables. (Also Midterm 251 V2 MCQ 1.)
They are rigid processes that must be followed in order, from initiation to closure.
They are optional tools that project managers may use only in large projects.
They are specific deliverables required at the end of each project phase.

questions.p: Engagement with stakeholders is weak, so requirements come in wrong and planning is built on bad information. What does this show about performance domains?
o: Each domain can be managed in isolation
That’s exactly what the example disproves.
Every domain is critical to the outcome.
They are interdependent: a problem in one spreads to the others
Domains run concurrently and affect each other.
They run one after another, like phases

questions.p: A PM has a flawless schedule, but a key department keeps blocking the project. What does the slide suggest is most needed?
o: The slide says these may matter even more than technical PM skills when working with stakeholders.
The plan isn’t the problem. A better chart won’t change how the department behaves.
The way of building isn’t what’s blocking the project.
Money doesn’t address a relationship problem.

questions.p: Many scope changes keep arriving from stakeholders. According to the checking-outcomes table, what might this indicate?
o: That’s a different outcome, checked in a different domain.
Stakeholders aren’t aligned with the project objectives
A high number of changes is the evidence used to check agreement on objectives.
Scope changes say nothing good about the baseline.
Changes don’t show whether opponents exist.

questions.p: Which is a desired outcome of the Team performance domain?
o: Fixed delivery dates for every release
That’s a schedule constraint, not a team outcome.
Leadership skills shown only by the PM
The domain deliberately says all members, not one person.
Leadership and interpersonal skills shown by all team members
The outcome covers everyone, not just the PM.
A team working without shared ownership
Shared ownership is one of the listed outcomes.

questions.p: Influencing, motivating and listening to the team are examples of which kind of activity?
On a project with centralized management, who usually carries accountability?
o: A rotating facilitator belongs to distributed management.
The customer isn’t accountable for managing the project.
That describes shared work, not centralized accountability.
One individual, such as the project manager
Centralized means being answerable sits with one assigned person.

questions.p: What gives a PM approval to form the team and use resources?
o: That analysis tells you whose interests matter, not who is authorized.
A project charter or other authorizing document
This is the document that formally authorizes the PM.
A burndown chart shows work remaining.
A risk register records risks. It authorizes nothing.

questions.p: A team has no designated PM. One member runs discussions this month, and another may next month. What is this person?
o: A sponsor funds and supports a project from outside the team.
The scenario says there is no designated PM.
A facilitator enables communication, collaboration and engagement, and the role can shift.

questions.p: In distributed management, leadership is limited to the person who is the facilitator.
o: Distributed management shares activities, and leadership belongs to everyone.
Leadership should be practiced by all team members.

questions.p: In decentralized project management, decision-making authority is primarily:
o: Distributed among team members to encourage shared accountability.
Concentrated in the hands of a single project manager.
Transferred to external auditors for oversight.
Reserved exclusively for senior executives in the organization.

questions.p: Which is a characteristic of decentralized management, according to the table?
o: Authority at the top of the chain of command
Faster decision making but more expensive

questions.p: During a retrospective, the team notes what went well and sets goals to improve. Which aspect of team development is this?
o: Growth means identifying strengths and areas to improve.
